summary: This work benchmarks repetition-code-based readout error detection and correction across IBM Heron r1–r3 superconducting processors and Quantinuum H1–H2 trapped-ion devices, varying code distance, hardware generation, and encoding layout. Both error detection (unanimous-vote decoding with post-selection) and correction (majority-vote decoding) improve readout fidelity on every device tested, but the benefit of larger code distances depends strongly on the underlying hardware: on superconducting processors, encoding gate errors offset gains rapidly, whereas trapped-ion devices' lower two-qubit gate error rates allow larger codes to remain advantageous.
motivation: Readout errors dominate noise in current quantum processors and limit sampling-based applications, but unlike conventional mitigation schemes that correct only aggregate statistics, shot-by-shot readout error mitigation could yield individually corrected samples. The relative performance of repetition-code methods across qualitatively different hardware platforms and successive hardware generations remained unexplored.
method: The authors implemented $[n,1]$ repetition-code encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors using $n-1$ CNOT gates in star or chain layouts, then compared unencoded baselines against unanimous-vote decoding (post-selecting shots where data and ancilla qubits agree) and majority-vote decoding (correcting every shot) while varying code distance and input state.
result: Error detection improved readout fidelity on all devices; for random/all-ones inputs on superconducting devices, benefit saturated at $[2,1]$ due to gate error accumulation, while on trapped-ion devices $[3,1]$ codes provided further gains. Post-selection retention fell to ~4% for $[4,1]$ on 24 qubits (IBM Pittsburgh) versus >90% on Quantinuum H1-1 (6 qubits). Majority-vote correction on the chain layout degraded fidelity on superconducting hardware but improved it on trapped-ion devices.
